prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: a neighbour's house flooded last winter. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 0)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a neighbouring property has flooded in winter, I should assume the source may be a burst pipe, overflowing guttering or surface water before I jump to flood as the cause. Early cause-checking helps me triage cover and urgency more accurately."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the report mentions repeated water ingress from next door, I should ask whether the neighbour’s property is still wet, whether any stop tap was accessible and whether emergency services or the local water undertaker were contacted. Those details often change the likely cause and the next step."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the damage is to a shared wall or adjoining ceiling, I should look for evidence of one-sided staining, damp patches and a clear start point rather than assume the whole area was affected at once. That usually tells me whether the event was sudden escape of water or a slower seepage."},{"type":"preference","content":"When policyholders are worried about flood, I prefer to separate emotional concern from actual evidence and ask for simple indicators like tide, river, surface run-off, blocked drains or snowmelt. That keeps the triage focused and avoids overcalling a flood claim."},{"type":"observation","content":"When a neighbour’s house flooded last winter, I should remember that cold weather increases the chance of frozen or split pipes and delayed discovery. Even small delays can turn a contained leak into a bigger internal damage claim."},{"type":"fact","content":"When there is mention of contents damage at the boundary of two homes, I should check whether water migrated through the party wall or under flooring, as that can affect the extent of visible loss. Hidden spread is common and can be missed if I only assess the obvious room-by-room damage."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the claimant says the neighbour has already arranged repairs, I should still capture before-and-after evidence and not rely only on verbal summaries. Photos, timelines and contractor notes are especially useful for delegated authority decisions."},{"type":"preference","content":"When I see signs of recurring seepage rather than a single sudden incident, I prefer to flag it for a more cautious review because gradual damage can fall outside the expected pattern for an escape of water claim. That reduces the risk of authorising the wrong class of loss."},{"type":"fact","content":"When winter flooding is localised to one adjoining property and nearby homes are unaffected, I should consider whether the cause is internal plumbing or drainage within that property rather than a wider weather event.
